subject: biochemistry
title: Neurochemistry: blood-brain barrier transport, myelin lipids, and glutamate excitotoxicity

steps.tx: The **blood-brain barrier** protects neural parenchyma from systemic fluctuations, toxins, and peripheral neurotransmitters. It is formed by non-fenestrated brain capillary endothelial cells linked by complex tight junctions (claudin-5 and occludin), supported by pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Lipophilic molecules like oxygen, carbon dioxide, and ethanol cross freely by simple diffusion. In contrast, essential water-soluble nutrients require dedicated transport carriers: glucose crosses via facilitated diffusion through **GLUT1**, while large neutral amino acids use LAT1.
steps.say: The blood-brain barrier consists of continuous capillary endothelium sealed by tight junctions and astrocyte foot processes. Lipophilic gases diffuse freely, while glucose crosses via GLUT1 and neutral amino acids via LAT1 transporters.

rows: Induces tight junction formation and neurovascular coupling
Actively pumps lipophilic xenobiotics back into blood

steps.tx: **Myelin** is an electrical insulator generated by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. It possesses an exceptionally high lipid-to-protein ratio (80 percent lipid to 20 percent protein). Characteristic myelin lipids include galactosylceramide, sulfatides, and plasmalogens. In multiple sclerosis, autoimmune CD4 T-cell infiltration and autoantibodies destroy myelin basic protein and proteolipid protein, slowing saltatory conduction and causing focal neurological deficits.
steps.say: Myelin insulates axons with an eighty percent lipid composition rich in galactosylceramides and sulfatides. Synthesized by oligodendrocytes in the brain and Schwann cells peripherally, autoimmune destruction of myelin proteins causes multiple sclerosis.

nodes.label: Autoimmune T-cell crossing of disrupted BBB
Targeting of myelin basic protein and PLP
Focal neurological deficits in multiple sclerosis

steps.tx: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, but excessive synaptic accumulation causes lethal **excitotoxicity**. Following release, glutamate is cleared from the synaptic cleft into astrocytes by excitatory amino acid transporters (EAAT2). Within astrocytes, glutamine synthetase converts glutamate into non-toxic glutamine, which is safely shuttled back to neurons. In acute cerebral ischemia, ATP depletion halts glial EAAT2 transport, causing massive extracellular glutamate accumulation.
steps.say: Glutamate is cleared from synapses by astrocyte EAAT2 transporters and converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase. In stroke, ATP exhaustion reverses glutamate uptake, flooding synapses and triggering neurotoxic calcium overload.

rows: Massive Ca2+ influx activates calpains and nNOS
Depolarizes membrane to relieve Mg2+ block on NMDA
Inactivated by oxidative stress, elevating free glutamate

steps.tx: Massive synaptic glutamate over-activates **NMDA** receptors, relieving the physiological magnesium block and flooding neurons with toxic amounts of calcium. Intracellular calcium overload activates calpains, caspases, phospholipase A2, and neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS), generating reactive peroxynitrite and triggering apoptosis. Neuroprotective NMDA antagonists like memantine provide symptomatic cognitive stabilization in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease without blocking physiological basal synaptic transmission.
steps.say: Excessive glutamate drives calcium through NMDA receptors, activating destructive proteases and nitric oxide synthase to cause neuronal necrosis. Memantine is an uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist used to stabilize Alzheimer disease.

nodes.label: Sustained toxic Ca2+ influx via NMDA receptors
Activation of calpain proteases and nNOS
Neuronal necrosis and penumbral infarct expansion
